text.p: U.S. microprocessor supplier Intel Corp on Wednesday launched its latest superchip, which it said would bring television-quality video, stereo surround sound and snappy three dimensional graphics to personal computers (PCs).

Trumpeting the new MMX chip as a "very big leap forward" for personal computer users, European technology directorIan Wilson told Reuters that the new technology could boost processor performance by 60 percent.
"On average, you're going to see a 60 percent increase in performance over the previous Pentium processor," he said.

The MMX chip will initially be offered with the 166 and 200 MHz Pentium processors and will combine high-performance local processing and storage with an Internet link. Having worked closely with key retailers across the world, Wilson said there would be a rapid increase in availability of systems using the new Pentium processor with MMX technology from the first quarter of this year.
"By end of year, a significant percentage of our micoprocessors being shipped will be incorporating MMX technology," he said.

While Wilson declined to comment on expected sales of the new chip, analysts have estimated that Intel could sell 30 million to 45 million MMX chips this year -- about half of the microprocessor units it will sell this year.
The new technology will also allow business users relatively low-cost video-conferencing over existing telephone lines.
Intel expects systems incorporating the new technology to be retailed at between $1,500 to $2,000.

"What has made PCs attractive to the home and consumer user has been the multimedia and communications capabilities," Wilson said. "People are widely using electronic mail, people are using the Internet access to the World Wide Web for shopping or booking holidays."
"The new features we have introduced with MMX technology allow a much better, richer multi-media experience...and we'll see a home and consumer demand for PCs growing even more."

Intel chips have been the leading industry standard for PC manufacturers and software developers and the company said it expected the Intel architecture, now extended by MMX technology, to also become industry standard.
